about: A fifth answer choice for each bank question the two practice exams use (five choices on the exam, four in the practice bank; needs-author mcq-options). examVersion (scripts/lib/apmicro-exams.mjs) puts each one in at a fixed position from the question id, with its explanation, which names the slip. The bank questions keep their four options.

mic-scarcity-4.option: Flour is a free good, so it has no price
mic-scarcity-4.why: Flour has a price because it is scarce; the recipe is the one that many can use at once without using it up.

mic-scarcity-2.option: No: scarcity ends once wants are met by income
mic-scarcity-2.why: Her wants and her time still outrun what she has; scarcity applies to every person, firm and society, whatever its income.

mic-economic-systems-15.option: Command economies coordinate by prices; markets by plans
mic-economic-systems-15.why: That is reversed: markets coordinate through prices, and command economies through a central plan.

mic-production-possibilities-17.option: Bowed out, because apps are easier to build than games
mic-production-possibilities-17.why: Getting faster at apps lowers the games given up per app, which is decreasing opportunity cost: a PPC bowed in, not out.

mic-production-possibilities-16.option: Resources are equally useless for both goods
mic-production-possibilities-16.why: A straight PPC means resources are equally suited to both goods, so each extra unit has the same opportunity cost.

mic-comparative-advantage-15.option: She has the absolute advantage in legal work too, so she types
mic-comparative-advantage-15.why: Absolute advantage does not decide who should type; her time typing costs her legal work, so the assistant has the comparative advantage.

mic-cost-benefit-11.option: As a sunk cost she can ignore
mic-cost-benefit-11.why: The rent she gives up is a cost she pays every month she keeps the shop, so it is an implicit cost, not a sunk one.

mic-marginal-analysis-15.option: Each extra unit costs more than the last
mic-marginal-analysis-15.why: That describes rising marginal cost; diminishing marginal utility is about satisfaction: each extra unit adds less.

mic-demand-15.option: Her rising cost of making pizza at home
mic-demand-15.why: The idea is about Lena’s extra satisfaction from each slice, not a cost; falling marginal utility explains why she pays less for the third.

mic-demand-14.option: Other things equal, a higher income lowers the quantity demanded
mic-demand-14.why: The law of demand links a good’s own price to its quantity demanded; income shifts demand instead.

mic-supply-16.option: It shifts right as the farmer earns more from soybeans
mic-supply-16.why: A higher soybean price makes corn the costlier use of the land, so the farmer supplies less corn at each price.

mic-price-elasticity-demand-11.option: It falls at first and then rises again near the bottom
mic-price-elasticity-demand-11.why: Along a straight downward demand line the elasticity falls steadily as the price falls; it does not turn back up.

mic-price-elasticity-demand-9.option: Percent change in total revenue divided by percent change in price
mic-price-elasticity-demand-9.why: The total revenue test uses elasticity, but the elasticity itself is the percent change in quantity demanded over the percent change in price.

mic-price-elasticity-supply-13.option: Sellers face less competition as time passes
mic-price-elasticity-supply-13.why: Competition is not the reason; over time firms can add workers, machines and plants, so output responds more.

mic-other-elasticities-13.option: Income and cross-price elasticities are smaller than 1
mic-other-elasticities-13.why: The size does not decide it: the sign of income and cross-price elasticity names the kind of good or relationship, so it is kept.

mic-other-elasticities-11.why: That is the cross-price elasticity; a response to pay is the income elasticity, the percent change in quantity over the percent change in income.

mic-equilibrium-surplus-16.option: A rule the government uses to ration the coffee
mic-equilibrium-surplus-16.why: No one set this price; it rose in the market and signals growers to plant more and buyers to use less.

mic-disequilibrium-changes-15.option: The quantities of X and Y rise by the same amount
mic-disequilibrium-changes-15.why: Elastic supply lets Y's output rise a lot, while X's inelastic supply sends most of its demand increase into price, so the quantity of Y rises more.

mic-government-intervention-23.option: The price falls to the level of 600 tons on supply
mic-government-intervention-23.why: Cutting the quantity to 600 tons moves the market up the demand curve, so buyers pay a higher price, not a lower one.

mic-trade-policy-20.option: A tariff raises imports; a quota lowers them
mic-trade-policy-20.why: A tariff raises the domestic price, so quantity supplied rises and quantity demanded falls: imports fall under a tariff too.

mic-production-function-10.option: It falls, because the shop now has more capital to pay for
mic-production-function-10.why: The cost of presses does not set marginal product; with more presses per worker, each worker adds more output.

mic-production-function-13.option: The firm’s profit at each level of output
mic-production-function-13.why: Profit needs prices and costs; a production function links inputs to output only.

mic-short-run-costs-7.option: Average fixed cost rises as output grows
mic-short-run-costs-7.why: AFC falls as output grows, and fixed cost does not affect MC; MC rises because each added worker adds less output.

mic-long-run-costs-4.why: Lowest LRATC is at about 300 to 400 kayaks a year per firm, so 30,000 kayaks take about 75 to 100 such firms.

mic-long-run-costs-17.option: A market with thousands of firms of many sizes
mic-long-run-costs-17.why: If the lowest-cost size is half the market, two or so firms can produce at minimum cost: a few large firms, not thousands.

mic-types-of-profit-12.option: It adds the value of the owner’s time to revenue
mic-types-of-profit-12.why: Economic profit subtracts the owner’s forgone earnings as an implicit cost; it does not add them to revenue.

mic-types-of-profit-15.option: The price rises as buyers compete for scooters
mic-types-of-profit-15.why: Economic profit draws new firms in, which adds supply and pushes the price down, not up.

mic-types-of-profit-18.option: The profit left after implicit costs are added to revenue
mic-types-of-profit-18.why: Implicit costs are subtracted, not added; normal profit is zero economic profit, which covers every cost including the owner’s best alternative.

mic-profit-maximization-8.option: a loss equal to its fixed cost
mic-profit-maximization-8.why: With price at the lowest point of ATC, revenue covers every cost including fixed cost: zero economic profit, not a loss.

mic-profit-maximization-5.option: \$1.60, the price minus the average cost
mic-profit-maximization-5.why: \$20 - \$18.40 = \$1.60 is the profit per mug; average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, \$100 ÷ 5 = \$20, the price.

mic-firm-decisions-16.option: It raises its price by the rent divided by output
mic-firm-decisions-16.why: A competitive firm takes the price, and a fixed cost does not change MC, so neither price nor output changes in the short run.

mic-imperfect-competition-12.option: It lies below demand, and so does a competitive firm’s MR
mic-imperfect-competition-12.why: A competitive firm sells any amount at the market price, so its MR is the horizontal price line, not below its demand.

mic-imperfect-competition-15.option: Rail cars are a public good, so no buyer pays for them
mic-imperfect-competition-15.why: Rail cars are rival and excludable; the barrier here is economies of scale, which give a small entrant a higher ATC.

mic-imperfect-competition-11.option: raise its output while keeping its price
mic-imperfect-competition-11.why: Its demand curve slopes down, so it can sell more only by lowering its price.

mic-monopoly-4.why: Area a is consumer surplus, above the price; total revenue is price times quantity, areas b and c.

mic-monopoly-12.option: Lowers the price and leaves the ferry with a profit
mic-monopoly-12.why: At the socially optimal price, P = MC, which is below ATC for a natural monopoly, so the ferry runs at a loss.

mic-monopoly-23.option: produce more and raise its price
mic-monopoly-23.why: Moving down its demand curve to sell more means a lower price, not a higher one.

mic-monopolistic-competition-20.option: Zero economic profit in the short run
mic-monopolistic-competition-20.why: Short-run profit can be positive for both; what they share is a downward-sloping demand curve.

mic-oligopoly-game-theory-17.option: the rival is most likely to choose
mic-oligopoly-game-theory-17.why: A dominant strategy is about the player’s own payoffs: it does better than its other strategies whatever the rival does.

mic-factor-markets-7.option: A new road brings more buyers from other towns
mic-factor-markets-7.why: More buyers raise the demand for boats and so for welders; the plant closing lowers boat demand and, through MRP, welder demand.

mic-factor-markets-19.option: A bakery sells a cake to a café
mic-factor-markets-19.why: That is a product market sale; a factor market trades inputs such as labor, as when the café hires a barista.

mic-factor-demand-supply-7.option: It has shifted right, because developers are easier to hire
mic-factor-demand-supply-7.why: MRP depends on marginal product and the product’s price; labor demand fell, so each developer’s MRP fell and the curve shifted left.

mic-factor-demand-supply-20.option: The wage falls and employment stays the same
mic-factor-demand-supply-20.why: Cheaper substitute machines lower the demand for operators, so along an upward labor supply both the wage and employment fall.

mic-competitive-factor-markets-17.option: Hire her if her MRP is above the average MRP
mic-competitive-factor-markets-17.why: The rule is marginal: hire while MRP is at least MRC (the wage), and \$95 is above \$80.

mic-monopsony-20.option: It raises employment in both markets
mic-monopsony-20.why: In a competitive market a wage floor above equilibrium cuts the quantity of labor demanded, so employment falls there.

mic-market-efficiency-18.option: Its MSB is below its MSC, so the quantity is right
mic-market-efficiency-18.why: If MSB were below MSC the unit should not be made; below the efficient quantity, MSB is above MSC.

mic-externalities-9.why: Those are external costs on units the efficient quantity keeps or that private surplus offsets; the deadweight loss is the triangle a.

mic-public-goods-16.option: It becomes excludable, because tolls are charged
mic-public-goods-16.why: A toll road was already excludable; congestion changes rivalry, since each extra car slows the others.

mic-intervention-structures-20.option: Keep firms from earning any accounting profit
mic-intervention-structures-20.why: Regulation aims at competitive price and output; firms can still earn an accounting profit and a normal profit.

mic-inequality-19.option: It moves below the line of equality for the first time
mic-inequality-19.why: A Lorenz curve already lies below the line of equality; more progressive taxes and transfers move it closer to the line.

mic-scarcity-16.option: The cost is the textbook money plus her time tonight
mic-scarcity-16.why: Money already spent is a sunk cost: it is gone whatever she does tonight, so it is not part of the opportunity cost.

mic-economic-systems-12.option: They make each good free for the people who need it
mic-economic-systems-12.why: Property rights do not make goods free; they let owners keep what they earn, which gives them a reason to produce and trade.

mic-economic-systems-2.option: Laws that fix the output of each firm
mic-economic-systems-2.why: Fixing output by law is a command method; in a market economy prices coordinate buyers and sellers.

mic-production-possibilities-18.option: It moves the firm to a point inside the curve for good
mic-production-possibilities-18.why: Building machines this year adds capital, so later the whole curve shifts out; producing inside the curve today is a choice, not a lasting effect.

mic-comparative-advantage-14.option: Both gain if the faster baker makes the pies
mic-comparative-advantage-14.why: With the same opportunity cost there is no comparative advantage, so specializing and trading creates no gain.

mic-comparative-advantage-13.option: To make a little of many goods yourself
mic-comparative-advantage-13.why: That is the opposite of specializing, which is focusing production on a few goods and trading for the rest.

mic-cost-benefit-12.option: The profit it earns after paying its costs
mic-cost-benefit-12.why: Profit is benefit minus cost; the total benefit of selling is the revenue itself.

mic-marginal-analysis-17.option: Buy one more of each with money she saves
mic-marginal-analysis-17.why: Her whole budget is spent, so she has no money left over; she raises utility by moving dollars from concerts (18) to books (30).

mic-demand-18.option: It raises the cost of building new apartments
mic-demand-18.why: Property rights do not add a building cost; they let owners keep the gains from buying, improving and selling, which is the incentive.

mic-supply-15.option: The bakery’s fixed cost rises with each extra loaf
mic-supply-15.why: Fixed cost does not change with output; the extra loaves cost more because overtime and a rented oven raise marginal cost.

mic-supply-14.option: Other things equal, a higher price raises the quantity demanded
mic-supply-14.why: That swaps the sides of the market; the law of supply is about the quantity sellers offer.

mic-price-elasticity-demand-14.option: It falls, because buyers now spend less on snacks
mic-price-elasticity-demand-14.why: A new substitute nearby makes buyers more willing to switch away when the theater’s price rises, so demand becomes more elastic.

mic-price-elasticity-supply-11.option: Paper napkins made in a plant with spare capacity
mic-price-elasticity-supply-11.why: Spare capacity lets output rise quickly, so supply is elastic; a small fishing fleet cannot catch much more within a week.

mic-price-elasticity-supply-8.option: Price divided by quantity supplied, at one point
mic-price-elasticity-supply-8.why: Elasticity compares two percent changes: the percent change in quantity supplied over the percent change in price.

mic-other-elasticities-16.option: It is positive, so the goods are complements
mic-other-elasticities-16.why: Gasoline up and trucks bought down gives a negative cross-price elasticity; a negative value means complements.

mic-equilibrium-surplus-15.why: Producer surplus is the price received minus the least the seller would accept: \$20 - \$12 = \$8.

mic-equilibrium-surplus-13.option: The quantity where buyers spend the most
mic-equilibrium-surplus-13.why: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, not where spending is largest.

mic-disequilibrium-changes-12.option: Supply shifts right to meet demand
mic-disequilibrium-changes-12.why: A price below equilibrium causes a movement along the curves, not a shift; quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

mic-government-intervention-22.option: A surplus of bus tickets, because buyers pay less
mic-government-intervention-22.why: A ceiling above the market price does not bind, so the price stays at \$2.00 with no shortage and no surplus.

mic-trade-policy-18.option: Its own producers have the absolute advantage
mic-trade-policy-18.why: If domestic producers made it at lower cost the domestic price would be lower; it imports because others have the lower opportunity cost.

mic-production-function-4.option: It is a short-run decision, because one field is still fixed
mic-production-function-4.why: With the lease the owner can change fields as well as pickers and crates; when every input can change, it is the long run.

mic-production-function-14.option: rise, because the new mechanic adds to total output
mic-production-function-14.why: Total product rises, but when the added output is below the average, the average is pulled down.

mic-short-run-costs-10.option: AFC and ATC shift up, but MC does not change
mic-short-run-costs-10.why: Flour is a variable cost: it raises MC, AVC and ATC, and leaves fixed cost and AFC as they were.

mic-long-run-costs-7.option: fall, because diseconomies of scale set in
mic-long-run-costs-7.why: Diseconomies of scale raise LRATC; on the falling part of the curve the firm has economies of scale.

mic-long-run-costs-14.option: Diminishing returns lower costs; diseconomies raise them
mic-long-run-costs-14.why: Both raise cost; the difference is that diminishing returns need a fixed input (short run) and diseconomies come from growing every input.

mic-types-of-profit-6.why: Firm Y earns 400 - 250 - 100 = 50 above all costs, an economic profit, so only Firm Z fits; Firm Z’s implicit costs turn its accounting profit into an economic loss.

mic-types-of-profit-10.option: The interest she pays on a loan for her chair
mic-types-of-profit-10.why: Interest she pays is money paid out, an explicit cost; the salary she gives up is the implicit one.

mic-profit-maximization-13.option: the extra cost of making one more unit
mic-profit-maximization-13.why: That is marginal cost; marginal revenue is the extra revenue from selling one more unit.

mic-firm-decisions-6.option: Produce: its price covers ATC at 100 jobs
mic-firm-decisions-6.why: ATC is \$12 and the price \$10, so it does not cover ATC; it produces because the price is above AVC, losing \$200 rather than \$400.

mic-firm-decisions-18.option: The part below the lowest point of AVC
mic-firm-decisions-18.why: Below minimum AVC the firm shuts down and supplies nothing; the supply curve is MC above minimum AVC.

mic-perfect-competition-16.option: Downward sloping, as larger firms get cheaper
mic-perfect-competition-16.why: In a constant-cost industry, entry does not change input costs, so long-run supply is horizontal at minimum ATC.

mic-imperfect-competition-8.option: Economies of scale that let one salon serve the whole county
mic-imperfect-competition-8.why: Salons are small and easy to open; their market power comes from differentiated styles and locations.

mic-imperfect-competition-16.option: Its demand is perfectly elastic at the market price
mic-imperfect-competition-16.why: Perfectly elastic demand describes a price taker; profit lasts here because barriers to entry keep rivals out.

mic-imperfect-competition-10.option: A product that buyers can compare easily across sellers
mic-imperfect-competition-10.why: Easy comparison helps buyers switch, which does not keep rivals out; a patent gives one firm the legal right to sell.

mic-imperfect-competition-19.option: Economies of scale from its many small mines
mic-imperfect-competition-19.why: Owning the key resource is what keeps rivals out here, not the size or number of its mines.

mic-monopoly-21.option: The part where marginal revenue is negative
mic-monopoly-21.why: Where MR is negative, cutting output would raise revenue and lower cost, so a monopolist with positive MC never stays there.

mic-monopoly-22.option: produces more and charges the same price
mic-monopoly-22.why: A monopoly restricts output to where MR = MC, below the competitive quantity, and so charges a higher price.

mic-price-discrimination-4.option: Student sales would rise and profit would stay the same
mic-price-discrimination-4.why: Students’ demand is more elastic, so a higher price cuts their purchases sharply and the cinema loses that profit.

mic-oligopoly-game-theory-13.option: Each firm sells a product with no close substitutes
mic-oligopoly-game-theory-13.why: That describes a monopoly; oligopolists watch rivals because each firm’s choice changes the others’ profits.

mic-factor-markets-14.option: It shows the wage the firm pays each worker
mic-factor-markets-14.why: The wage is set in the labor market; the MRP curve shows each added worker’s value to the firm, which is why it is labor demand.

mic-factor-markets-15.option: It falls, because the firm needs fewer hours of work
mic-factor-markets-15.why: MRP is marginal product times marginal revenue; the machine raises each worker’s marginal product, so MRP rises.

mic-factor-markets-20.option: It falls for the last worker and stays the same for the rest
mic-factor-markets-20.why: MRP is marginal product times marginal revenue; a lower price lowers marginal revenue, so MRP falls for every worker.

mic-factor-demand-supply-18.option: It increases at first and then falls below where it began
mic-factor-demand-supply-18.why: Cheaper drones mean more drones, each needing a driver, so demand for the complement, drivers, rises; nothing here turns it back down.

mic-competitive-factor-markets-20.option: The firm sets the wage for its own workers
mic-competitive-factor-markets-20.why: A firm in a competitive labor market is a wage taker; it pays the market wage for each added worker, so MFC equals the wage.

mic-monopsony-9.option: hires more workers and pays a higher wage
mic-monopsony-9.why: The monopsonist hires where MRP = MFC, to the left of the competitive quantity, and pays the lower wage read from labor supply.

mic-market-efficiency-6.why: Areas b and c are part of the subsidy’s cost that goes to buyers and sellers; the deadweight loss is the triangle g past the efficient quantity.

mic-market-efficiency-20.option: Efficiency rises, because the floor ends the shortage
mic-market-efficiency-20.why: A binding floor sits above equilibrium and creates a surplus, not a shortage; trade falls below the efficient quantity.

mic-externalities-22.option: MPC lies above MSC, so the quantity is too low
mic-externalities-22.why: With a negative production externality MSC is above MPC, and the market overproduces at too low a price.

mic-public-goods-15.option: A rival good, because each car uses up road space
mic-public-goods-15.why: One more car slows no one, so the uncrowded road is nonrival; the toll gate makes it excludable: a club good.

mic-intervention-structures-18.option: It falls, because the subsidy raises its fixed cost
mic-intervention-structures-18.why: A per-unit subsidy lowers marginal cost, so MR meets MC at a larger quantity: output rises.
